children: Shares of digital banking platform Nubank

jumped 5.8% in the afternoon session after UBS analyst Thiago Batista raised the company’s price target to $20.50 from $18.20 while maintaining a Buy rating. According to StreetInsider, UBS raised Nu’s price target by $2.30 while keeping its Buy recommendation, implying roughly 40% upside from recent trading levels. The higher target refreshes UBS’s valuation framework on the Latin American digital bank without changing the firm’s already constructive stance.

That backdrop matters because Nu’s most recent results showed the business converting scale into earnings: roughly 139 million customers globally, FX-neutral revenue near $5.9 billion, first-time net income of $1.1 billion, and ROE around 33%, with Brazil still the core franchise and Mexico expanding as a full-scale digital bank. Against that setup, the UBS move reads as a valuation catch-up to Nu’s profitability trajectory rather than a fresh upgrade in rating.
What Is The Market Telling Us

Nubank’s shares are quite volatile and have had 15 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 6 days ago when the stock dropped 3.4% on the news that September consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7% and core inflation topped estimates, reigniting concerns over Federal Reserve interest rate hikes. The hotter-than-expected data showed headline consumer prices rising 3.7% annually, while core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, reached 2.6%. In the wake of the report, traders raised the implied probability of a central bank rate increase at the next meeting to nearly 44%. The sudden shift in policy expectations pushed Treasury yields higher and triggered volatility across bond markets. Banking leaders pointed out that persistent interest rate uncertainty and Treasury market swings are dampening client trading activity and stalling corporate dealmaking as reported by TheStreet. When borrowing costs remain high and unpredictable, corporations typically hold off on mergers, acquisitions, and debt offerings, creating broad sector-wide pressure on investment banking revenue.

Nubank is down 9.7% since the beginning of the year, and at $15.37 per share, it is trading 18.1% below its 52-week high of $18.76 from January 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Nubank’s shares at the IPO in December 2021 would now be looking at an investment worth $1,487.
